cases.answer: Last spring my unit switched to a new bedside barcode medication system with only a week's notice, and I was the night nurse picked to learn it first and then teach the others. I learned that teaching something is the fastest way to be sure you really know it.

cases.answer: Before I teach anything I check the teaching sheet is the current one for that patient's diagnosis. During the session I use teach-back: I ask the patient to explain the insulin steps or the warning signs in their own words, and I correct what is missing. Afterwards I chart what I taught, who was present and how well they repeated it back in the electronic health record. This matters because a patient who misunderstands discharge instructions can end up back in hospital, and the family at home is the one left coping. If I find a gap I go back that shift, tell my charge nurse and suggest changing the handout so the same mistake does not recur.

cases.answer: Last winter I was the staffing coordinator on a surgical floor and I learned on a Thursday that two of our float shifts for the weekend had been cancelled because of a budget freeze. I pulled together the census forecast and three options, such as moving one nurse from the medical unit or closing two beds, and I asked the four charge nurses to meet me for ten minutes that afternoon. I told them plainly what had been cut, said I knew it was frustrating, and went through the options. By Friday noon we had agreed to borrow one nurse, and Saturday ran without an unsafe ratio. I learned to tell people early, even when I do not have every answer.

If a patient told me they did not want to follow the low-salt diet teaching I had given, I would first sit down and ask what worries them, without interrupting. Often it is about food they love or a story from a relative, and I want to hear that before I explain anything. Then I would explain the reasons in plain words and offer a smaller step, such as cutting back on one salty food. The cost is that we might go slower than the ideal plan, and I would accept that if it means they will actually try it. I would speak to the patient directly, then document their wishes and what I taught, and ask the dietitian to see them again before discharge so they can follow up.
